steps.text: Pour cold water into a bowl; add gelatin and let stand until softened, about 5 minutes.

Beat 1/2 cup of sugar, egg yolks, lemon juice, and salt together in a bowl until smooth. Cook in the top of a double boiler, stirring constantly, until it is the consistency of custard. Add grated lemon zest and softened gelatin and stir thoroughly; set aside to thicken and cool, about 10 to 15 minutes.
Beat egg whites in a glass, metal, or ceramic bowl until foamy. Gradually add remaining 1/2 cup of sugar, continuing to beat until soft peaks form; fold egg whites into cooled custard mixture.
Pour filling into prepared pie shell and chill in refrigerator until firm, at least 2 hours. Garnish with sweetened whipped cream if desired.

raw_recipe.headline: Lemon Chiffon Pie
raw_recipe.description: This lemon chiffon pie is light and fluffy with a creamy filling made with gelatin, lemon zest, lemon juice, egg yolks, and whipped egg whites.

review.reviewBody: I actually have this recipe from an old cookbook. The only difference is that in that cookbook, they also add 1/2 cup of orange juice (and 1/2 tsp. of EACH orange and lemon zest, instead of just the 1 tsp. lemon zest). It is called citrus chiffon pie and has been my husband' favorite for 20 years. I use a regular pie crust as I find the the graham is too heavy (in texture and taste) for this sort of fluffy pie... and yes I have used the premade kind of crust when I am lazy...which is more often than not! I also cut the 1/2 sugar to 1/3 when you whip the whites to keep it sort of tart (the addition of orange isn't as sour). The orange + the lemon give it a very good flavor. Way better than lemon meringue with that pesky, squeaky meringue on top. I almost always use fresh lemon and orange juice, but have used the bottled kind and it is still good (just skip zest). I try to stick with organic if using zest, though.

I have always made this with cornstarch instead of gelatin, and the cornstarch is cooked into the custard at the beginning. Then I beat the egg whites and sugar and fold them into the custard while it is still hot. This cooks the raw egg white, and I have never had a problem with it. Basically you make a lemon meringue pie, but instead of putting the meringue on top, you fold it into the lemon custard, then chill.

Have made it four times now - fourth try included 6 eggs, 8 oz. lemon juice, 1 tablespoon lemon zest. Topped with fresh, sweetened whipped cream (8 oz. heavy cream with 1/4 cup powdered sugar - added after you've whipped the cream to almost done). I'm sticking with this version.

I like the general simplicity of this recipe, but do find it irresponsible to publish without some updating for health concerns. It asks you to make a basic raw egg meringue to fold into the pie, and even provides a warning at end of recipe that may be ‘harmful’ to elderly, pregnant women, or compromised people. I suggest if you follow this recipe, adjust for the meringue part by making an ‘Italian Meringue’ with ingredients they call for, then folding that into yolk mixture. An easy search will help you find the technique. If that had been suggested and included from the start in this recipe my review would have been 5 stars. It’s a little fussier, but still an easy technique, that will ensure all parts of the eggs are safely cooked. Then you can enjoy the nostalgic dessert safely, as it is worth it. It’s okay to update Classic recipes, especially for safety that we often ignored in the past.

Giving it a 5 star, just 'cause I know next time I make it that's what it'll be. Not sure what I did or didn't do, but it would never get thick. I finally added a little corn starch and beat it with electric mixer while over double boiler. Also, unlike impatient me, you must let it cool pretty well before adding the whites, else it all gets a bit runny. After cooling in fridge for awhile was ok. I did make a gluten-free pie crust. Think I agree with other reviewer & will make whites into soft peaks instead of stiff.
I do love the lemon, so will try again (& again!!:)

I’ve made this particular pie for over 56 years. Its so light and delicious with a delicate lemon flavor. The hand written one I have, has waded over the years. So decided to look for something close ion the internet. Found yours. It’s very close, however I don’t use the gram-cracker crust! It’s far to strong a flavor for this delicate pie. Please recommend regular pie crust or the pre made shortbread crust. They let the light lemon flavor shine.
I used Splenda Stevia in place of the sugar and a regular pie crust. I added more than 1 tsp rind, to increase the 'bite'. With the Stevia it was a nice light lemon pie that was not too sweet.

1. The phrase "until it is the consistency of custard" in the recipe confused me. I thought that I was supposed to cook it until it had the consistency that a custard has when you serve it (i.e., once it's set), and then you were supposed to let it thicken even more. But that results in overcooking, and a texture that doesn't combine well with the gelatin. In hindsight, I realized that what the recipe meant was that you cook until you have the consistency of an unset custard, one that has just been cooked but hasn't been allowed to thicken. I wish there was some more precise way of specifying this, because I feel getting this right is the key to the recipe working out. 2. The original Duncan Hines recipe says that you should let the gelatin DISSOLVE in the cold water. This recipe only says that you should SOFTEN the gelatin. I did that, but the softened gelatin didn't fully mix with the custard (though part of the problem was the overcooking), resulting in chunks in the final product. In hindsight, you should DISSOLVE the gelatin completely. 3. The original Duncan Hines recipe calls for a "pinch of salt"; the web says a "pinch" is technically 1/16 of a teaspoon. This recipe calls for 1/2 teaspoon. I feel that 1/2 teaspoon is way too much for such a delicate pie. I used a rough pinch. 4. If one is bothered by egg whites (I am disgusted by uncooked egg), one can replace each egg white by 2 tsp meringue powder and 2 tbsp water (according to Wilton). The result whipped very nicely.
I followed the filling directions and put it in a regular crust (homemade of course) it turned out great!

I followed the instructions exactly, and it turned out pretty great.

The lemon flavor in this pie is really light and delicate. The people I made it for liked that about it--they kept saying how lemon desserts are usually too strong for their taste, and they liked how light this one was. If you wanted a stronger flavor, you could probably just use extra lemon juice.

I didn't have any problem getting the custard to thicken--you just have to give it time to cool down. If you need/want to speed it up, refrigerate it. I put mine in an ice-bath in the refrigerator because I was short on time, and it thickened in the time it took to make the meringue. In retrospect, I wish I had just put it in the refrigerator without the ice bath, because the custard around the edges thickened quicker than the rest of it. Or perhaps it would have worked better to put it in an ice bath and stir it while it cooled. Next time, I'll just budget more time for it to cool and thicken.

One issue I had was with the texture of the gelatin. It was clumpy after softening in the water, and then I feel like it didn't mix into the custard evenly, even after several minutes of thorough stirring. This may be user error on my part, because I've never worked with gelatin before (aside from making jello). I accidentally let it sit in the cold water for longer than 5 minutes, so maybe that was my mistake. But regardless, I'd appreciate a little more detail in the instructions.
